overview: This atlas label combines ancient farming horizons with a language-family hypothesis; it names no single people or state. Its 2000 to 323 BCE window is approximate. The earliest outline even reaches Afghanistan, while later shapes spread across mainland Southeast Asia and southern China. These are not verified language boundaries; some examples lie outside particular snapshots. Named Vietnamese and Thai sites below illustrate regional lives, without identifying every resident as an Austroasiatic speaker.

periods.title: Diverse early farming communities
periods.summary: Rice and millet appear together in northern Vietnam, alongside older ways of obtaining food. The map begins after some regional Neolithic developments were already underway.

periods.title: Coastal homes and exchanged grain
periods.summary: Southern Vietnamese communities built durable floors and ate combinations of cereals and local resources; Rach Nui probably obtained grain through exchange.

periods.title: Metalworking and unequal communities
periods.summary: Bronze technology and contrasting burial wealth mark regional changes. These approximate boundaries organize examples, not the lifespan of a unified kingdom.

sections.title: How a rice harvest leaves clues

items.text: At An Son and Loc Giang in southern Vietnam, early Neolithic potters mixed rice-processing remains into clay. A 2017 study scanned small pottery samples in three dimensions and found husks and grain-attachment parts inside. An everyday broken pot had become a tiny archive of farming.

The telling detail was a rough, deeply recessed scar at the base of a rice spikelet. Wild rice usually releases its grains naturally; domesticated plants hold on until people remove them. These scars helped identify cultivated rice, rather than merely proving that someone had collected a wild plant.

These southern settlements also yielded stone adzes, bone tools, decorated pottery and remains of domestic pigs and dogs. Postholes and prepared floors locate wooden buildings on mounds above low-lying landscapes. Food production belonged to a wider household world of building, making tools and tending animals.

sections.title: More than a bowl of rice

items.text: Around 2000 BCE, the Trang Kenh community near Ha Long Bay used rice and foxtail millet. Researchers identified microscopic plant traces, including silica bodies called phytoliths and starch grains. These little survivors can reveal food processing even when no recognizable meal remains on a plate.

Nearby island sites Bai Ben and Bai Cat Don tell a different food story. Traces include taro, yams, acorns, palm, ginger and beans, as well as millet. Their inhabitants continued using diverse plants while incorporating cereals. The neighbors did not all receive the same prehistoric dinner menu.

At Rach Nui, around 1500 to 1300 BCE, rice and millet occurred alongside abundant remains of other plants. Researchers also found evidence of fishing, hunting and gathering. Living permanently in a village did not require everyone to become a specialist rice farmer.

Rach Nui stood beside a salty, tidal environment, a difficult setting for rice cultivation. Archaeologists propose that residents acquired cereals from other communities while drawing heavily on local resources. Rice-processing debris shows handling at the settlement; it does not by itself locate the fields where the crop grew.

sections.title: Homes, floors and the work of keeping house

items.text: At Loc Giang, floor builders probably burned shells to make lime, then prepared hard mortar surfaces. Excavators found more than thirty stacked surfaces, dating roughly from 1560 to 1200 BCE. This was skilled construction with recipes for materials, not simply packing down whichever dirt happened to be underfoot.

Microscopic study of Loc Giang floors found little accumulated debris, while worn areas had been repaired. Researchers interpret this as regular cleaning and maintenance, perhaps sweeping or using mats. Someone had to keep the household floor usable; the evidence does not preserve a chore chart assigning the job.

At Lo Gach in southern Vietnam, woven mats left impressions on clay floors about 2750 years before 1950, roughly 800 BCE. The mat itself could decay while its pattern survived. Such traces bring weaving and furnishings into view alongside the more durable stone and pottery.

Man Bac in northern Vietnam preserves an unusually personal story from around 2000 to 1700 BCE. A man known to archaeologists as Burial 9 developed severe physical disabilities during childhood and survived into his twenties. Researchers infer sustained assistance from others over approximately a decade.

His movement restrictions imply help obtaining food and water, and probably assistance with eating and drinking. The study also argues that maintaining his cleanliness required bathing and help with toileting. These are reasoned reconstructions of care needs, not proof of a particular toilet, hospital or medical profession.

The same case makes cooperation visible: moving him safely and keeping him sheltered took repeated attention. Archaeology cannot tell us the names or family relationships of his helpers. It can show why a community’s achievements include care for a person, as well as the tools and buildings it made.

sections.title: Changing technology, status and living languages

items.text: Bronze brought new expertise in combining and casting metals. A 2015 radiocarbon study favored an eleventh-century BCE Bronze Age transition at Ban Non Wat in northeastern Thailand, substantially later than some older chronologies. The timing is an archaeological argument, not a birthday shared by all the communities in this atlas shape.

At Ban Non Wat, some early Bronze Age graves held striking quantities of valuables, including rich infant burials. Researchers interpret this as evidence for inherited status. Burial 197 also contained a pottery vessel decorated with dancers: a lively little scene among the axes and other offerings.

A later language glimpse: modern Khmer writes ទឹក, transcribed tɨk, meaning “water.” This is a SEAlang dictionary witness checked in 2026, from a resource based mainly on 1977 and 1997 dictionaries. It is not prehistoric writing. The ancient sites here have no securely identified inscription establishing their residents’ languages.

ending.text: The atlas stops this label in 323 BCE, not at a documented collective collapse. Austroasiatic languages continue in diverse communities, including Khmer, Vietnamese, Mon and several Indian language groups. Later states have their own histories; neither rice cultivation nor a language family makes them one continuing empire.
